hello.title: Hello, C
hello.summary: Write your first C program, print text with `printf`, and learn how to compile and run it.
hello.lesson.0: Every C program starts in a function called `main`. Here is a complete program that prints one line of text.
hello.lesson.2: The first line, `#include <stdio.h>`, loads the **standard input and output** library. A file that ends in `.h` is called a **header**. It contains `printf`, the function that prints text. Without it, the compiler does not know `printf`.
hello.lesson.3: `int main(void)` is where the program starts. `void` in the parentheses means that `main` takes no input. The curly braces `{` and `}` hold its statements, and every statement ends with a semicolon `;`. `return 0;` ends `main` and tells the system that the program finished without errors.
hello.lesson.5: C is a **compiled** language: a program called a **compiler** translates your source code into a file that the computer can run. Save the code as `hello.c`. The command `cc hello.c -o hello` compiles it, and `-o hello` names the result `hello`. Then `./hello` runs the program.
hello.lesson.6: The compiler checks your code before anything runs. If it finds a mistake, it prints an error with the file name and the line number, for example `hello.c:4:5: error`. Fix the first error first: the errors after it are often caused by it.
hello.lesson.8: `printf` does not start a new line by itself. Inside a string, `\n` is the **newline** character. Without it, the next output continues on the same line.
hello.lesson.11: The backslash `\` starts an **escape sequence**, a special character inside a string. `\n` is a new line, `\t` is a tab, `\"` is a double quote, and `\\` is a backslash.
hello.lesson.13: C is case-sensitive: `Main` or `Printf` do not work. If you forget a `;`, the compiler stops with an error.
hello.card.1: `int main(void) { ... }` is where the program starts
hello-1.explain: The function is called `printf`, all in lower case, and text must be inside double quotes.
hello-2.explain: The first `printf` does not end the line, so `Sam!` continues right after `Hi, `.
hello-3.prompt: These lines are inside `main`. What do they print?
hello-3.explain: Only the last string contains `\n`, so all four letters end up on the same line.
hello-4.statement: `return 0;` at the end of `main` tells the system that the program finished without errors.
hello-4.explain: The value that `main` returns goes back to the system. `0` means success.
hello-5.prompt: Fill the gap so the program can use `printf`.
hello-5.explain: `printf` is declared in the header `<stdio.h>`, the standard input and output library.
hello-6.prompt: Fill the gap so the output is on two lines.
hello-6.explain: The newline character is written with a backslash: `\n`. `\t` is a tab, not a new line.
hello-7.prompt: Build a line that prints `Hi!` and ends the line.
hello-7.explain: First comes the function name `printf`, then the text in parentheses, and a `;` at the end.
hello-8.prompt: Put the lines in order so the program prints `Ready` and then `Go`.
hello-8.explain: The `#include` comes first, then `main`. Statements run from top to bottom, and `return 0;` ends the program.
hello-9.prompt: Match the code to its meaning.
hello-10.explain: The statement on line 3 has no `;` at the end. Write `printf("Hello\n");`.
hello-11.explain: `\"` is an escape sequence: it puts a double quote into the string. The backslash itself is not printed.
hello-12.statement: `Printf("Hi\n");` also prints `Hi`, because C ignores upper and lower case.
hello-12.explain: C is case-sensitive. The function is called `printf`, all in lower case.
variables.title: Variables and types
variables.summary: Store numbers and characters in variables of type `int`, `double` and `char`, and print them with `printf`.
variables.lesson.0: A **variable** is a named place in memory that stores a value. In C, every variable has a **type**, and you write the type before the name. `int age = 30;` creates a variable `age` of type `int`, a whole number, with the value `30`.
variables.lesson.2: `printf` can print values, too. Its first argument is the **format string**. Each **format specifier** in it, like `%d`, is a placeholder: `printf` replaces it with the next value after the comma. `%d` stands for an `int`.
variables.lesson.4: `double` stores numbers with a decimal point, and `char` stores a single character in single quotes, like `'A'`. Each type has its own specifier: `%d` for `int`, `%f` for `double` and `%c` for `char`. You can put several specifiers in one format string. The values follow in the same order.
variables.lesson.6: `%f` prints six digits after the decimal point. Write `%.2f` to get two digits; the value is rounded. Use `%%` to print the percent sign itself.
variables.lesson.9: The `=` sign **assigns** a value: it stores the value on the right in the variable on the left. You can assign a new value later, but the type stays the same. You can also declare a variable first and give it a value later.
variables.lesson.11: Write `const` before the type when a value must never change. The compiler then stops with an error if you try to assign a new value. In the next example, `*` means multiply.
variables.lesson.13: A variable without a value contains garbage: whatever was in that memory before. Always give a variable a value before you read it. Also make sure the specifier matches the type: printing a `double` with `%d` gives wrong output.
variables.card.0: `int n = 5;` whole number, `double x = 2.5;` decimal, `char c = 'A';` character
variables-1.explain: `double` stores numbers with a decimal point. An `int` would lose the `.75`, and a `char` stores one character.
variables-2.prompt: These lines are inside `main`. What do they print?
variables-2.explain: `b = a` copies the value `4` into `b`. Changing `a` later does not change `b`.
variables-3.prompt: These lines are inside `main`. What do they print?
variables-3.explain: `%.1f` prints one digit after the decimal point and rounds: `72.349` becomes `72.3`.
variables-4.explain: `%f` without a precision always prints six digits after the decimal point.
variables-5.prompt: Fill the gap so the program prints `B`.
variables-5.explain: A single character goes in single quotes. `"B"` in double quotes is a string, and `B` without quotes would be a variable name.
variables-6.prompt: Fill the gap so the program prints `7`.
variables-6.explain: `%d` is the format specifier for an `int`. `%f` is for `double` and `%c` is for `char`.
variables-7.prompt: Declare a constant `max` with the value `100`.
variables-7.explain: `const` comes before the type, then the name, `=` and the value. One `=` assigns, `==` would compare.
variables-8.prompt: Put the lines in order so the program prints `15`.
variables-8.explain: A variable must be declared before you use it: first `price`, then `total`, which uses `price`, then the output.
variables-9.prompt: Match the format specifier to what it prints.
variables-10.prompt: The program should print `9.99`. Which line has the bug?
variables-11.explain: `%.2f` always prints exactly two digits after the decimal point, even when they are zeros.
variables-12.statement: After `const int max = 10;`, you can write `max = 20;` later in the program.
variables-12.explain: A `const` variable cannot get a new value. The compiler stops with an error.
operators.title: Operators
operators.summary: Calculate with `+`, `-`, `*`, `/` and `%`, understand integer division, and use `++`, `+=` and casts.
operators.lesson.0: C has the usual arithmetic operators: `+` adds, `-` subtracts, `*` multiplies and `/` divides. As in mathematics, `*` and `/` come before `+` and `-`. Use parentheses `(` `)` to change the order.
operators.lesson.3: When both numbers are `int`, `/` is **integer division**: the result is a whole number, and the part after the decimal point is cut off. `7 / 2` is `3`, not `3.5`. The **remainder operator** `%` gives what is left over: `7 % 2` is `1`.
operators.lesson.5: If at least one number is a `double`, the division keeps the decimals, as `7.0 / 2` shows. The remainder `%` only works with whole numbers. It tells you if a number is even: `n % 2` is `0` for every even `n`.
operators.lesson.7: Changing a variable based on its own value is very common, so C has short forms. `x += 5` means `x = x + 5`. There are also `-=`, `*=`, `/=` and `%=`. `x++` adds 1 to `x` (**increment**), and `x--` subtracts 1 (**decrement**).
operators.lesson.9: Use `++` and `--` as statements of their own, like `count++;`. Inside bigger expressions they are hard to read, and some combinations, like `i++ + i++`, are not allowed in C and give unpredictable results.
operators.lesson.11: Sometimes you have two `int` values but want a result with decimals. A **cast** converts a value to another type: write the type in parentheses before the value, like `(double)total`. Converting a `double` to an `int` cuts off the decimals.
operators.lesson.13: `(double)(total / count)` is `3.0`, not `3.5`: the division inside the parentheses happens first, with whole numbers. Cast before you divide.
operators-1.prompt: These lines are inside `main`. What do they print?
operators-1.explain: Both numbers are `int`, so `/` is integer division: `17 / 5` is `3.4`, and the `.4` is cut off.
operators-2.prompt: These lines are inside `main`. What do they print?
operators-2.explain: `5` fits into `17` three times, which makes `15`. The remainder is `17 - 15`, so `2`.
operators-3.explain: `n += 3` makes `n` equal to `7`, and `n *= 2` doubles it to `14`.
operators-4.explain: The cast turns `9` into a `double` before the division, so the result keeps its decimals.
operators-5.explain: With two `int` values, `/` cuts off the decimals, so `10 / 4` is `2`.
operators-6.prompt: Fill the gap so the program prints `3.5`.
operators-6.explain: The cast `(double)` turns `a` into `7.0` before the division. A cast needs the parentheses.
operators-7.prompt: Fill the gap so `count` grows by 1.
operators-7.explain: `count++` adds 1 to `count`. `count--` would subtract 1, and `+=` needs a value on its right.
operators-8.prompt: Write a statement that adds `10` to `total`.
operators-9.prompt: These lines are inside `main`. Put them in order so the program prints `2`.
operators-9.explain: Each line uses the variable from the line before: `each` is `3`, and `left` is `17 - 15`, so `2`.
operators-10.prompt: The program should print `2.50`. Which line has the bug?
operators-10.explain: `cost / 2` is integer division and gives `2` before the value is stored. Write `double half = cost / 2.0;`.
operators-11.prompt: Match the operator to its meaning.
operators-12.statement: `-7 / 2` is `-3` in C, because integer division cuts off the decimals.
operators-12.explain: `-7 / 2` would be `-3.5`. Integer division cuts off the `.5`, so the result is `-3`.
conditions.title: Decisions
conditions.summary: Make decisions with `if`, `else` and `switch`, compare values, and combine conditions with `&&`, `||` and `!`.
conditions.lesson.0: An `if` statement runs code only when a **condition** is true. The condition goes in parentheses, the code in curly braces. With `else`, you say what happens otherwise.
conditions.lesson.2: C compares with `==` (equal), `!=` (not equal), `<`, `>`, `<=` and `>=`. A comparison gives `1` when it is true and `0` when it is false. In a condition, `0` means false and every other number means true.
conditions.lesson.4: Do not confuse `=` and `==`. `if (x = 5)` does not compare: it assigns `5` to `x`, and the condition is always true. The compiler warns about it, so read the warnings.
conditions.lesson.6: Chain conditions with `else if`. C checks them from top to bottom and runs only the first block whose condition is true.
conditions.lesson.9: `&&` means **and**: both sides must be true. `||` means **or**: at least one side must be true. `!` means **not**: it turns true into false and false into true.
conditions.lesson.12: `switch` compares one whole number or character with several fixed values. Each `case` is a value followed by a colon. `break` ends the `switch`. Without it, the program **falls through** and also runs the next case. `default` runs when no case matches.
conditions.card.4: `0` is false, every other number is true
conditions-1.prompt: These lines are inside `main`. What do they print?
conditions-1.explain: `12 > 25` is false, so C checks the next condition. `12 > 10` is true, so it prints `Mild` and skips the rest.
conditions-2.prompt: These lines are inside `main`. What do they print?
conditions-2.explain: `3 < 2` is false, but `5 == 5` is true. With `||`, one true side is enough, and a true comparison gives `1`.
conditions-3.explain: In a condition, `0` means false. So the `else` block runs.
conditions-4.prompt: Which condition is true when `x` is between 1 and 10, both included?
conditions-4.explain: Both comparisons must be true, so you need `&&`. `1 <= x <= 10` does not work in C: it compares the result `0` or `1` of `1 <= x` with `10`.
conditions-5.explain: A single `=` assigns: `x` becomes `0`, and the condition is always false. To compare, write `x == 0`.
conditions-6.prompt: Fill the gap so the program prints `Even`.
conditions-6.explain: `n % 2 == 0` is true when the remainder is `0`, which means the number is even.
conditions-7.prompt: Fill the gap so the program prints only `Small`.
conditions-7.explain: `break` ends the `switch`. Without it, the program falls through and also prints `Large`.
conditions-8.prompt: Write the first line of an `if` that checks whether `age` is at least 18.
conditions-8.explain: The condition goes in parentheses after `if`, and the block starts with `{`. "At least" means `>=`.
conditions-9.prompt: Put the lines in order: the program prints `Hot` above 25, `Warm` above 15 and `Cold` otherwise.
conditions-9.explain: Each `printf` goes right after the condition it belongs to. The `else` block comes last, because it runs when no condition is true.
conditions-10.prompt: The program should print nothing. Which line has the bug?
conditions-10.explain: `code = 3` assigns instead of comparing, so the condition is always true. Write `if (code == 3) {`.
conditions-11.prompt: Match the operator to its meaning.
conditions-12.statement: Without `break`, a `case` in a `switch` also runs the code of the next case.
conditions-12.explain: This is called fall-through. The program continues with the next case until it reaches a `break` or the end of the `switch`.
loops.title: Loops
loops.summary: Repeat code with `for`, `while` and `do`-`while`, and control loops with `break` and `continue`.
loops.lesson.0: A **loop** repeats code. The `while` loop checks its condition before every round and runs the body as long as the condition is true.
loops.lesson.2: If the condition never becomes false, the loop runs forever. Make sure the body changes something the condition depends on, like `n--` above.
loops.lesson.4: A `for` loop puts everything for counting in one line, with three parts separated by `;`: the start (`int i = 1`), the condition (`i <= 3`) and the step (`i++`). The step runs after each round. The variable `i` exists only inside the loop.
loops.lesson.6: The step can be any change, like `i += 2` or `i--`. A loop can also build a result: here `sum` starts at `0`, and every round adds the current number.
loops.lesson.9: A `do`-`while` loop checks the condition **after** the body. So the body always runs at least once, even if the condition is false from the start. Note the `;` after the condition.
loops.lesson.12: `break` leaves the loop immediately. `continue` skips the rest of the current round and goes on with the next one.
loops.card.3: `break` leaves the loop, `continue` skips to the next round
loops-1.prompt: These lines are inside `main`. What do they print?
loops-1.explain: The loop adds `1`, `2`, `3` and `4` to `total`, which makes `10`.
loops-2.prompt: These lines are inside `main`. What do they print?
loops-2.explain: `n` becomes `3`, `9`, `27` and `81`. Then `n < 50` is false and the loop stops.
loops-3.explain: A `do`-`while` loop runs the body once before it checks the condition. Then `6 < 3` is false, so it stops.
loops-4.prompt: Which loop prints the numbers from 1 to 5 in increasing order?
loops-4.explain: The loop starts at `1` and runs as long as `i <= 5`, so `5` is included. `i < 5` would stop at `4`.
loops-5.statement: A `do`-`while` loop always runs its body at least once.
loops-5.explain: The condition is checked after the body, so the body runs once even when the condition is false from the start.
loops-6.prompt: Fill the gap so the loop prints `0`, `1` and `2`.
loops-6.explain: `i < 3` is true for `0`, `1` and `2`. With `<=`, the loop would also print `3`.
loops-7.prompt: Fill the gap so the loop stops when `i` reaches `4`.
loops-7.explain: `break` leaves the loop at once, so the program prints `1`, `2` and `3`. `continue` would only skip `4`.
loops-8.prompt: Build a `for` loop header that counts from `10` down to `1`.
loops-8.explain: The loop starts at `10`, runs as long as `i >= 1`, and `i--` makes `i` smaller after each round.
loops-9.prompt: These lines are inside `main`. Put them in order so the program prints `3`, `2` and `1`.
loops-9.explain: `n` must exist before the loop. Inside the loop, print `n` first and then make it smaller.
loops-10.prompt: These lines are inside `main`. Which line has the bug?
loops-10.explain: A `do`-`while` loop ends with a `;` after the condition. Write `} while (n < 3);`.
loops-11.prompt: Match the code to its meaning.
loops-11.pairs.0: counts with start, condition and step
loops-11.pairs.2: checks the condition after the body
loops-12.prompt: These lines are inside `main`. What do they print?
loops-12.explain: When `i` is `3`, `continue` skips the `printf` and the loop goes on with `4`.
functions.title: Functions
functions.summary: Split programs into functions with parameters and return values, declare them with prototypes, and understand scope.
functions.lesson.0: A **function** is a named block of code that you can call again and again. You already know two: `main` and `printf`. A function definition starts with the **return type**, then the name and the **parameters** in parentheses.
functions.lesson.2: `int square(int n)` says: the function is called `square`, it takes one `int` called `n`, and it gives back an `int`. `return` ends the function and hands the value back to the caller. The value you pass in the call, like `4`, is called an **argument**.
functions.lesson.4: Separate several parameters with commas. If a function returns nothing, its return type is `void`. If it takes nothing, write `void` in the parentheses, as in `main(void)`.
functions.lesson.7: C reads a file from top to bottom, so you must declare a function before you call it. If you want to define it below `main`, put a **prototype** above `main`: the first line of the function, ending with `;`.
functions.lesson.10: Parameters and variables declared inside a function are **local**: they exist only inside that function, from their declaration to the closing `}`. The same is true for variables declared inside any block, such as a loop. So different functions can use the same names without conflict.
functions.lesson.11: C passes arguments **by value**: the function gets a copy. If it changes its parameter, the variable of the caller stays the same.
functions.lesson.13: To change a variable of the caller, a function needs the address of that variable. You will learn how in the unit about pointers.
functions.card.1: `void` means no return value, `(void)` means no parameters
functions.card.2: `int max(int a, int b);` is a prototype above `main`
functions.card.3: Arguments are copied, local variables live only in their block
functions-2.explain: The arguments are matched by position: `a` is `3` and `b` is `8`, so the result is `3 - 8`.
functions-3.explain: `reset` gets a copy of `score`. It sets its copy to `0` and prints it, but `score` in `main` stays `42`.
functions-4.prompt: What is the return type of a function that returns nothing?
functions-4.explain: `void` means "no value". Such a function does not need a `return` statement with a value.
functions-5.statement: A function must be declared before the line where you call it.
functions-5.explain: C reads the file from top to bottom. Define the function above the call, or put a prototype there.
functions-6.prompt: Fill the gap so `half` gives back its result.
functions-6.explain: `return` ends the function and hands the value back to the caller.
functions-7.prompt: Fill the gap with the prototype for `cube`.
functions-7.explain: A prototype is the first line of the function, with the return type, and it ends with `;`.
functions-8.prompt: Build the first line of a function `area` that takes two `double` values and returns a `double`.
functions-8.explain: The return type comes first, then the name, then the parameters with their types, separated by a comma.
functions-9.prompt: Put the lines in order so the program prints `10`.
functions-9.explain: The header comes first because `show` uses `printf`. `show` is defined before `main` calls it.
functions-10.explain: `add` must give back a value, but it never returns one. Write `return a + b;`.
functions-11.prompt: Match the code to its meaning.
functions-11.pairs.1: a function without a return value
functions-12.statement: A variable declared inside one function can also be used in another function.
functions-12.explain: Variables inside a function are local. They exist only in that function.
arrays.title: Arrays and strings
arrays.summary: Store many values in arrays, loop over them, and work with strings as `char` arrays using `string.h`.
arrays.lesson.0: An **array** stores several values of the same type, one after another. You write the size in square brackets `[ ]` and the values in curly braces. Each element has an **index**, starting at `0`: `scores[0]` is the first element.
arrays.lesson.2: An array with 4 elements has the indexes `0` to `3`. C does not check the index: `scores[4]` reads memory that does not belong to the array, and the program may crash or print garbage.
arrays.lesson.4: `sizeof` gives the size of something in bytes. `sizeof(scores)` is the size of the whole array and `sizeof(scores[0])` the size of one element, so dividing them gives the number of elements. The result has the type `size_t`, a whole number that is never negative. You print it with `%zu`.
arrays.lesson.6: If you list the values, you can leave out the size, as in `int scores[] = {90, 75, 82, 60};`. The compiler counts the values for you.
arrays.lesson.8: C has no separate string type. A **string** is an array of `char` that ends with the **null character** `'\0'`. A string literal like `"cat"` adds it automatically, so `char word[] = "cat";` uses 4 bytes. Print a string with `%s`.
arrays.lesson.10: The header `<string.h>` has functions for strings. `strlen(s)` counts the characters before the `'\0'`. `strcpy(dest, src)` copies the string `src` into the array `dest`. `strcmp(a, b)` compares two strings and gives `0` when they are equal.
arrays.lesson.12: You cannot copy strings with `=` or compare them with `==`. Use `strcpy` and `strcmp` instead. The target array must be big enough for all characters plus the `'\0'`.
arrays.card.1: `sizeof(a) / sizeof(a[0])` is the number of elements
arrays.card.2: `char s[] = "hi";` ends with `'\0'`, print it with `%s`
arrays-1.prompt: These lines are inside `main`. What do they print?
arrays-1.explain: Indexes start at `0`: `nums[1]` is `8` and `nums[3]` is `16`.
arrays-2.explain: `strlen` counts the characters before the `'\0'` at the end: `h`, `e`, `l`, `l`, `o`.
arrays-3.explain: The string `"dog"` has three letters plus the `'\0'` at the end, so the array has 4 bytes.
arrays-4.prompt: Which expression gives the last element of `temps`?
arrays-4.explain: An array with 5 elements has the indexes `0` to `4`. `temps[5]` is outside the array.
arrays-5.statement: `strcmp(a, b)` gives `1` when the two strings are equal.
arrays-5.explain: `strcmp` gives `0` when the strings are equal. That is why you write `strcmp(a, b) == 0`.
arrays-6.prompt: Fill the gap to print the string.
arrays-6.explain: `%s` prints a string. `%c` prints only one character.
arrays-7.prompt: Fill the gap so the program prints the sum `18`.
arrays-7.explain: `values[i]` is the element at the current index. `values[3]` would be outside the array.
arrays-8.prompt: Declare an array `primes` with the values `2`, `3` and `5`.
arrays-8.explain: The square brackets after the name make it an array, and the values go in curly braces.
arrays-9.prompt: These lines are inside `main`. Put them in order so the program prints `cat` and then `3`.
arrays-9.explain: First create the array, then copy the text into it. Then print the string and its length.
arrays-10.explain: Strings cannot be compared with `==`. Write `if (strcmp(answer, "yes") == 0) {`.
arrays-11.prompt: Match the code to its meaning.
arrays-11.pairs.1: marks the end of a string
arrays-12.statement: `char word[] = "sun";` creates an array with 4 elements.
arrays-12.explain: The three letters are followed by the null character `'\0'`, so the array has 4 elements.
pointers.title: Pointers and structs
pointers.summary: Use addresses with `&` and `*`, change variables through pointer parameters, and group data in a `struct`.
pointers.lesson.0: Every variable lives at an **address** in memory. The operator `&` gives the address of a variable. A **pointer** is a variable that stores an address: `int *p` declares a pointer to an `int`.
pointers.lesson.1: The operator `*` in front of a pointer **dereferences** it: it gives the value at that address. Through the pointer, you can read the variable and also change it.
pointers.lesson.3: The symbol `*` has several jobs. In a declaration, `int *p` means that `p` is a pointer. In an expression, `*p` means the value that `p` points to. And `a * b` is still a multiplication.
pointers.lesson.5: Remember that C copies arguments. If a function gets a pointer, it can change the caller's variable through it. You pass the address with `&`. In `add_one`, `(*n)++` needs the parentheses: it increases the value that `n` points to.
pointers.lesson.7: A pointer must point to a valid variable before you use `*` on it. Use `NULL` for a pointer that points nowhere, and never dereference a `NULL` pointer: the program crashes.
pointers.lesson.9: A `struct` groups several values, called **members**, into one new type. The definition ends with `};`. You reach a member with a dot, as in `p.x`.
pointers.lesson.11: With a pointer to a struct, use the arrow `->` to reach a member: `ptr->x` means `(*ptr).x`. Functions often take a pointer to a struct, so they can change it without copying it.
pointers.card.3: `struct Point { int x; int y; };` then `p.x`
pointers-1.prompt: These lines are inside `main`. What do they print?
pointers-1.explain: `p` points to `a`, so `*p = *p + 4` changes `a` itself from `3` to `7`.
